implementation_notes: Ruby has the virtual copy constructor built into the root class: `dup` allocates a new instance of the receiver's class and copies its instance variables (shallow), and `clone` does the same while additionally copying the singleton class and the frozen state; both funnel through `initialize_copy`, the per-class hook where deep copying of reference attributes belongs (`dup` also calls `initialize_dup`, `clone` calls `initialize_clone`). Nothing has to be declared, and polymorphic copy works automatically because the copy is of the runtime class even when the caller only knows a superclass. `dup` is the everyday choice (it does not carry frozenness or singleton methods); `clone(freeze: false)` is the faithful-but-unfrozen variant.
code_sketch:
class Shape
  attr_accessor :tags

  def initialize_copy(original)      # per-class deep-copy hook
    super
    @tags = original.tags.dup
  end
end

copy  = shape.dup                   # same class, shallow + initialize_copy
frozen = shape.freeze
frozen.clone(freeze: false).frozen? # => false; clone copies frozenness by default
pitfalls: `dup`/`clone` are shallow: instance variables referencing mutable objects are shared, so a copy without an `initialize_copy` that duplicates them aliases the original's arrays, hashes and nested objects.
`clone` copies the frozen state and singleton class, `dup` does not - using the wrong one either hands you a frozen copy or silently drops singleton methods and modules added with `extend`.

Frameworks redefine the semantics: ActiveRecord's `dup` clears identity/timestamps through its own `initialize_dup`, so `dup` on a domain object may intentionally drop state - check the class's `initialize_copy`/`initialize_dup` before relying on `dup` for a faithful clone.
